paras: The lynching of Charles Evans took place at Norway, Orangeburg County, South Carolina, early on July 1, 1903, when a white crowd took Evans, a Black man described as a "mulatto," from the town guardhouse, hanged him and shot his body. Evans was suspected of shooting John T. Phillips, a white Confederate veteran, at his supper table, and before the lynching the crowd whipped three or four other Black men. It drew notice because the Columbia State's correspondent said it came close to justifying lynching, and because Black residents' later gathering brought militia to the town.

According to The State, on June 27 two of Phillips' sons whipped Lorenzo Williams, a Black man said to have sworn at one of them, and Evans and his brother Jim, friends of Williams, protested and were said to have threatened the family. The paper complained that local Black people had been "trifling and impertinent," and described the Evans brothers as educated sons of a white man.

A little before 8 p.m. on June 29, a shot fired through a window struck Phillips at supper and wounded two of his children. By June 30 five Black men were under arrest, Evans as the chief suspect, and a Norway dispatch said all asserted their innocence. Armed farmers then poured into the town of about 200 people until the crowd passed 500.

Around 11 p.m. a Black courier said the farmers could come to the outskirts and "get" a man, and fifteen or twenty men went out, disarmed a group of armed Black men and locked them in the guardhouse. At about 2 a.m. the prisoners were "cowhided" one by one until, the State correspondent wrote, each named Charles Evans as the gunman. Evans was then hanged in woods outside town, told to "Ask Phillips" when he begged for mercy, and two hundred guns were fired, the correspondent wrote. Inquest witnesses found the body hanging from an oak, hands tied behind the back.

Governor D. C. Heyward telegraphed Sheriff Dukes and the coroner to pursue the lynchers. On July 2 a coroner's jury found that Evans died of gunshots and strangulation "at the hands of a party or parties unknown to the jury." No arrest for the lynching appears in the coverage, though in August a $500 reward stood for the conviction of those who lynched "Charlie Evans."

On July 4, at the mayor's request, fifty Columbia militiamen went to Norway after several hundred Black people gathered at Bush Pond and threatened five white men alleged to have been connected with the lynching. The troops left on July 5, the day Phillips died. An inquest into his death implicated Jim Evans and nine other Black men, and by July 13 the sheriff held ten for the killing or the "riot," while Jim Evans remained at large; no report of a trial was found.

Out-of-state white papers ran a short Columbia wire, headed "Lynched for Murder" in the New-York Tribune; the Montgomery Advertiser noted it was Governor Heyward's first lynching. In South Carolina the fullest account was Randolph W. Smith's for The State, reprinted under headlines such as "Maddened Citizens Avenge the Crime," which credited "the best citizens" with the beatings and called Evans a "cowardly brute." A State editorial took a different line, tracing both the murder and the lynching to a community's failure "to enforce the laws and decency."

Black weeklies carried only brief wire items: the Wichita Searchlight said Evans, "colored," was taken "from the jail," and the Baltimore Afro-American reported the militia call and a rumor of over 2,000 Black people surrounding the town. The Sedalia Times printed, in quotation marks, an editorial that set Norway beside the Evansville riot as "white savagery" and read the Black gathering as people who would "turn and fight."

Reports differ on the number whipped: three in the Tribune and The State, four in the Montgomery Advertiser and the Wichita Searchlight. First-day reports that the brother (called "Henry" in the Tribune) had surrendered at Orangeburg were contradicted by later ones saying he had not been found. The Montgomery Advertiser mentioned a "confession" by Evans, but the accusations reported by The State came from prisoners questioned under the whip.

reader.title: Lynching of Charles Evans
bases: A crowd of white men took Charles Evans from the Norway guardhouse, hanged him and shot his body, after whipping other Black prisoners (A2, A12, A13); the coroner's jury found he died by gunshots and strangulation at the hands of persons unknown (A18, A22).

Evans, held in the town guardhouse on suspicion of shooting John T. Phillips, was taken out by a large armed crowd, hanged and shot (A2, A11, A13); The State described it as the community having 'avenged' Phillips, and the coroner's jury found he was killed by 'parties unknown' (A10, A18, A22).

The Columbia wire (A2, A3), the State correspondent's on-scene account (A10, A13), the coroner's inquest testimony and verdict (A18, A22) and Black-press briefs (A28, A30) agree that Evans was taken from custody, hanged and shot.

accounts.label: Columbia State correspondent
accounts.gist: Traces the shooting to the Phillips sons' whipping of Lorenzo Williams and the Evans brothers' threats; describes armed Black men disarmed and cowhided into accusing the Evanses, then Evans hanged and riddled with 'two hundred guns'.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Six witnesses; body found hanging from an oak with hands tied; death by gunshots and strangulation at the hands of parties unknown.

accounts.label: Black weekly briefs
accounts.gist: Short wire items: Evans taken from jail and lynched, four prisoners beaten; militia sent after Black threats of revenge.

accounts.label: Editorial quoted in the Sedalia Times
accounts.gist: Pairs Norway with the Evansville riot; says the body was kept hanging a day as a warning and that Black residents, whipped and threatened, armed to defend themselves.

framing.detail: The State: 'Maddened Citizens Avenge the Crime'; 'the best citizens' beat the armed Black men; Evans a 'cowardly brute'; circumstances 'came so near justifying the crime'.
State editorial reprinted in Sumter traces murder and lynching alike to the community's failure to enforce the law, blaming the Evanses' white father.
Out-of-state papers ran the Columbia wire: 'Lynched for Murder' (Tribune), 'Alleged Murderer is Strung Up by a Mob' (Montgomery Advertiser).
Follow-ups called the Bush Pond gathering a threatened 'Negro Uprising'; a Mississippi paper called Evans a 'negro desperado' and blamed unrest on a 'Jim Crow' law.
Wichita Searchlight and Baltimore Afro-American ran short wire items without comment.
Sedalia Times printed an editorial on 'white savagery' reading the Norway gathering as Black self-defense.

record_check.dossier: Night of June 30-July 1; the crowd acted about 2 a.m. July 1 (the inquest says 'Tuesday night'). 1903-07-01 matches most reports.

record_check.record: Charles Evans, John Felder, Pink Hartwell, H. S. Johnson, Jim Evans, Phillips
record_check.dossier: Charles Evans (killed) and three or four unnamed whipped Black men. John Felder and H. S. Johnson appear in no article; Pink Hartwell was named at the Phillips inquest as implicated, not whipped; Jim Evans was accused and at large; Phillips was the white man shot.
No white person was hurt by the mob. In the precipitating shooting Phillips was wounded (died July 5) and two of his children were hit.
Coroner's verdict 'parties unknown'; The State describes white townspeople and farmers, 'the best citizens'; five named white men alleged to be connected.

record_check.record: seized a Black man who had shot a white man
record_check.dossier: Evans was accused of the shooting, on statements whipped prisoners gave; the papers report no trial. Armed Black residents gathered twice: on the night of the lynching (disarmed and whipped) and at Bush Pond July 4.
Confirmed: taken from the town guardhouse.

info: Lynching about 2 a.m., early Wednesday July 1, 1903 (the inquest calls it 'Tuesday night', i.e., night of June 30); the shooting of Phillips was about 8 p.m. Monday June 29.

Norway, Orangeburg County, S.C.; taken from the town guardhouse to woods outside town; body found hanging from an oak tree (200 yards from the Phillips house per The State; about a mile out of town per inquest testimony).
Charles (Charley) Evans, described as a 'mulatto', killed; three (or four) unnamed Black men whipped before the lynching.
Accused of shooting John T. Phillips, a white Confederate veteran, through his window at supper on June 29; his brother Jim was accused as an accessory.

White townspeople and farmers of Norway and the surrounding country, unnamed; The State spoke of 'the best citizens' and 'the people of Norway'; the coroner's jury found 'parties unknown'. Black residents later threatened five named white men alleged to be connected with the lynching.
Jim Evans reported to have surrendered at Orangeburg July 1, but later reports say he was never found; no trial report found.
